requirement:
Project definitions MUST NOT use a full name beginning with `habeas:`.
Validation MUST report a project definition that uses the reserved prefix under
{cite}`requirements.ci.identifiers`.
rationale:
structural: `requirements.references.builtin_definitions.reserved_names` states only observable behavior. The first clause, "Project definitions MUST NOT use a full name beginning with `habeas:`", constrains the input that projects may supply. The second clause, "Validation MUST report a project definition that uses the reserved prefix under `requirements.ci.identifiers`", requires a validation diagnostic. That diagnostic is output, and `requirements.ci.identifiers` is only cited to say which category the diagnostic falls under.

The text prescribes no library, algorithm, signature, type, field or named interface. Any implementation that rejects a `habeas:`-prefixed project definition and reports it under the identifiers requirement would satisfy it. For example, a check in a parser, in a separate validation pass, or in a shared name validator would all behave the same. So no clause makes a particular code structure mandatory.

No implementation roots were supplied, and none are needed as structural evidence. Whether the validation behavior actually works is a question for the behavioral and test criteria. It is not a structural obligation.

behavioral: The requirement has two obligations. (1) A project definition MUST NOT use a full name beginning with `habeas:`. (2) Validation MUST report such a definition, with the invalid-name handling from the cited `requirements.ci.identifiers`.

`tests/references.rs#fn[project_definitions_cannot_use_reserved_built_in_names]` is marked `{test}` for the subject. It covers both obligations:
- It writes a chapter file named `habeas:shadow.md` containing `{req} ready`, so the full name is `habeas:shadow.ready` and begins with the reserved prefix. It asserts that validation reports an invalid requirement name error saying names beginning with habeas: are reserved, with the right file.
- It also writes `{req} habeas:none` in `md/rules.md`, which gives `rules.habeas:none`, and asserts the matching error. That name does not begin with `habeas:` as a full name, so this case goes beyond the literal text. The assertion is extra evidence of rejection and does not contradict the requirement.
- The valid `ready` definitions sit in the same files as the invalid ones. The test checks that `habeas::status_markdown` does not list either invalid name as a requirement. That is the `requirements.ci.identifiers` outcome: an invalid name does not define a requirement.

I read `src/evidence.rs#fn[collect_definitions]` only to check for branches the text distinguishes. It applies one reserved-prefix check to requirements, examples and definitions alike. Only the noun in the message differs, so the text does not distinguish those kinds and no per-kind test is needed. The code has no other case split the requirement names.

I found no obligation that lacks a test.

text: Project definitions MUST NOT use a full name beginning with `habeas:`.
Validation MUST report a project definition that uses the reserved prefix under

Requirement and reference names MUST have nonempty dot-separated segments containing only ASCII letters, digits, underscores, or hyphens. A `{req}` directive whose full name is invalid, including one whose chapter path gives an invalid namespace, and a role with an invalid name MUST remain literal and MUST NOT define or reference a requirement. For nested chapter paths, a leading `reqs/` and a final `index` or `README` segment MUST be omitted from the requirement namespace.
Habeas MUST resolve built-in names of the form `habeas:<name>` alongside project
definitions in every project without a project declaration. Each built-in MUST
specify its permitted reference roles and have fixed text stating its obligations.
Habeas's reference documentation MUST include that text.
